title: DAVE3625 independent practice bank
notes: Practice topic weights and question-type ratios are design choices, not official exam predictions. Supplementary sources are explicitly labelled. Numerical families are sampled at most once per exam.

questions.prompt: In the grocery assignment, what do Grc_df.head(10) and Grc_df.tail(10) inspect?
options: The first ten and last ten rows
The ten largest and ten smallest sales automatically
Only rows with missing values
The first ten and last ten columns
questions.explanation: head and tail select rows by position; they do not sort values or filter nulls.

questions.prompt: Item_Fat_Content includes differently formatted names for the same category. What should precede comparing category frequencies?
options: Normalise equivalent labels consistently
Encode every spelling as a different ordered number
Scale the target to zero mean
Delete all rows in the largest category
questions.explanation: The assignment asks students to identify and fix inconsistent category representations before interpreting the data.

questions.prompt: What does concatenating two same-schema grocery DataFrames along rows usually do?
options: Stack their observations into one table
Match records by a shared key like a join
Compute each column's mean
Create supervised labels automatically
questions.explanation: Row-wise concatenation combines records; it differs from a key-based merge.

questions.prompt: After sorting Item_Outlet_Sales in ascending order, where is the smallest non-missing value?
options: At the beginning of the sorted non-missing values
At the end of the sorted non-missing values
Always at original index zero
It cannot be found without training a model
questions.explanation: Ascending order places smaller values first; original index labels need not change.

questions.prompt: The assignment bins Item_Weight and computes each bin's count and mean. What is the purpose?
options: Summarise how observations are distributed across weight intervals
Train a binary classifier without a target
Prove weight causes sales
Replace missing labels with bin numbers
questions.explanation: Binning and grouped aggregation provide descriptive summaries; they do not establish causation.

questions.prompt: What is the main distinction between SVC(kernel='linear') and SVC(kernel='rbf')?
options: The RBF kernel can express nonlinear boundaries in the original input space
The linear kernel needs no target labels
The RBF kernel always guarantees higher test accuracy
Both settings must produce the same boundary
questions.explanation: Kernel choice changes the model's representation and flexibility; select it with validation rather than assuming more flexibility is always better.

questions.prompt: Which comparison would fairly select between linear and RBF SVMs?
options: Use the same validation procedure with preprocessing fitted inside each training fold
Use whichever has the better final test score after unlimited tuning
Skip scaling for one model without checking its effect
Compare training accuracy only
questions.explanation: Consistent data handling and validation make algorithm comparisons meaningful while preserving final test independence.

questions.prompt: A lab defines passed = (final_grade ≥ 10). Keeping final_grade as a feature to predict passed before the exam creates what problem?
options: The feature directly reveals the target and is unavailable at the intended prediction time
A harmless increase in feature count
An unsupervised clustering problem
A guarantee of useful early intervention
questions.explanation: The target is derived from the final grade. Using it prospectively leaks the outcome instead of learning an early predictor.

questions.prompt: What modelling assumption distinguishes Gaussian Naive Bayes for numeric features?
options: Each feature has a Gaussian class-conditional distribution, alongside conditional independence
All classes must have identical means
It uses a nearest-centroid clustering objective without labels
It requires every feature to be binary
questions.explanation: GaussianNB models each feature's distribution within each class; its assumptions are approximations to be evaluated.

questions.prompt: Mandatory Assignment 2 asks for a stock's closing price on a given date. Which output formulation fits this request?
options: A numeric regression target
A cluster ID without labels
A binary spam label
A category inferred only from a filename
questions.explanation: The specified output is the closing-price value, so it is regression, even though related stock tasks can be classifications.

questions.prompt: The Ruter assignment predicts passenger count for a bus on a date. Which evaluation approach is appropriate for that numeric target?
options: Report numeric prediction error on held-out journeys or dates, with a baseline
Treat any R² value as a percentage of exactly correct counts
Use only a confusion matrix without defining count categories
Report training accuracy as the only measure
questions.explanation: A count prediction can be handled as regression. MAE or RMSE describes numeric error; a generic percentage accuracy is not automatically meaningful.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of pd.to_numeric(column, errors="coerce") on an unparseable value?
options: It becomes a missing numeric value
It becomes the column mean automatically
It is guaranteed to remain unchanged
It becomes the target label
questions.explanation: Coercion permits conversion but can silently increase missingness, so inspect the result.

questions.prompt: Why inspect null counts after coercing a numeric column?
options: To see how many values failed conversion
To fit the model's final weights
To prove all values are accurate
To change the training split automatically
questions.explanation: Type conversion can hide format defects by turning them into nulls; quantify and investigate those changes.

questions.prompt: What does value_counts(dropna=False) add compared with dropping null categories?
options: It includes missing values in the displayed frequency counts
It fills all missing values
It removes duplicate rows
It sorts observations by prediction probability
questions.explanation: Including nulls makes missingness visible in a categorical frequency summary.

questions.prompt: Why can a constant feature usually be removed from a predictive table?
options: It cannot distinguish among observations in that dataset
It guarantees a high positive correlation with every target
It always reveals a future outcome
It is the same as a missing target
questions.explanation: A feature with no variation provides no within-dataset discrimination, although its definition may still matter for documentation.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of separating numeric and categorical preprocessing branches?
options: Apply transformations suited to each feature type
Ensure all strings are interpreted as continuous quantities
Fit the final test set twice
Avoid specifying which columns are inputs
questions.explanation: A column transformer can apply imputation and scaling to numeric fields and encoding to categories.

questions.prompt: An encoder meets a new category during prediction. What should the pipeline have specified?
options: A consistent policy for unknown categories
A way to read the future target label
A requirement to fit on each test row
An instruction to silently reorder model inputs
questions.explanation: Deployment can contain categories absent during fitting. The pipeline needs a defined behaviour compatible with its learned representation.

questions.prompt: Why should test data use the training feature order and encoding?
options: The fitted model associates each input position with a particular feature
Any permutation of feature columns is always equivalent
The model automatically infers every column's semantic meaning
It allows target leakage
questions.explanation: A consistent schema prevents a valid-looking input matrix from being interpreted incorrectly.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with fitting separate standard scalers independently on train and test data?
options: The test data use a different learned coordinate system and influence preprocessing
It always improves generalisation
It is the required way to avoid leakage
It creates more labels
questions.explanation: The test set should be transformed with training-fitted parameters so the model sees a consistent representation.

questions.prompt: Which inspection can help reveal unusually skewed numeric values?
options: A histogram or box plot
The alphabetical order of field names
The number of Python imports
A list of predicted class names only
questions.explanation: Distribution plots reveal shape and extremes, helping choose suitable cleaning and transformation decisions.

questions.prompt: A standard logistic model without engineered nonlinear features produces what kind of boundary?
options: A linear boundary in its input feature space
An arbitrary cluster hierarchy
A guaranteed perfect circle in all datasets
A separate rule for every training row
questions.explanation: The linear score combined with a fixed probability threshold creates a linear decision boundary in the supplied features.

questions.prompt: What should be distinguished when a classifier reports probability 0.8?
options: A model estimate and a guaranteed truth
The training set and a PowerPoint filename
A cluster ID and a database row only
The file size and the number of classes
questions.explanation: An estimated probability can be wrong or poorly calibrated; it is not certainty about an individual outcome.

questions.prompt: Why does a smaller K often produce a more irregular KNN boundary?
options: Decisions depend on fewer nearby examples and local detail
It replaces the labels with a global mean
It ignores distances
It becomes a linear model by definition
questions.explanation: Small neighbourhoods respond to local variations, including noise.

questions.prompt: If a KNN binary vote ties, what is needed for a reproducible prediction?
options: A defined tie-breaking rule
A claim that ties are mathematically impossible
Removal of all training labels
An extra true label from the future
questions.explanation: A voting classifier must specify how to resolve equal support; the course's simple majority examples avoid ties.

questions.prompt: Why may reducing tree depth improve held-out accuracy while lowering training accuracy?
options: It trades some training fit for less sensitivity to noise
It gives the tree access to test outcomes
It ensures every leaf contains exactly one row
It converts the model into K-means
questions.explanation: Complexity control can improve generalisation even if the training score is lower.

questions.prompt: In an ordinary decision tree, what determines which branch a new input follows?
options: The input feature values and learned split tests
The unknown correct class supplied at prediction time
The final test-set score
The alphabetical order of target names only
questions.explanation: Inference follows the learned rules without needing the query's true label.

questions.prompt: Which is a meaningful comparison of KNN and decision trees?
options: KNN uses proximity to stored examples; a tree follows learned feature tests
Both always use identical distance formulas
Both require scaling for exactly the same reason
Neither can classify more than two classes
questions.explanation: These algorithms use different decision mechanisms and have different practical sensitivities.

questions.prompt: Why should classifier choice consider latency as well as predictive quality?
options: A model can be accurate but too slow for the intended workflow
The slowest model is always the most reliable
Latency replaces every need for accuracy
A larger model is necessarily faster
questions.explanation: The practical value of a model depends on operational constraints as well as evaluation scores.

questions.prompt: Why is raw cluster label 0 not inherently better or worse than label 1?
options: Cluster IDs are arbitrary identifiers, not ranks or known class meanings
Cluster 0 always contains errors
Cluster 1 always contains positives
The largest ID is the best group
questions.explanation: Renaming clusters does not change the underlying partition.

questions.prompt: Why can increasing K reduce K-means within-cluster squared distances without proving better clusters?
options: More centres can fit finer detail, including structure that is not useful
The objective directly measures every real-world use case
Every extra cluster supplies new target labels
K determines the number of available data rows
questions.explanation: A numerical compactness objective is not by itself a complete test of useful segmentation.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is correct?
options: K-means assigns by centres; DBSCAN can leave sparse observations as noise
DBSCAN requires a predefined K while K-means never does
Both must use manually supplied group labels
Both guarantee the same partition after scaling
questions.explanation: The algorithms encode different assumptions about what constitutes a group.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish the fraction of all examples that are mislabeled from the fraction of errors due to mislabels?
options: They use different denominators and answer different prioritisation questions
They are always numerically identical
Only the number of features affects either fraction
Neither quantity can be estimated
questions.explanation: A small fraction of all examples can account for a large share of the remaining evaluation error as a system improves.

questions.prompt: Two error categories overlap. Can their estimated independent ceilings simply be added to obtain a guaranteed joint improvement?
options: No; overlap can double-count errors and the fixes may interact
Yes; error categories are always disjoint
Yes; any ceiling is a guaranteed gain
No; categories cannot be counted
questions.explanation: Ceiling analysis requires attention to overlap and assumptions about what a fix changes.

questions.prompt: When choosing an improvement project, what complements its estimated error-reduction ceiling?
options: Implementation cost, feasibility and importance of the affected errors
Only how memorable the first failure was
Only the length of the project title
The assumption that every ceiling will be reached
questions.explanation: A large potential improvement may be expensive or infeasible; prioritisation combines impact estimates with practical judgement.

questions.prompt: A system predicts the majority class for every case and gets 95% accuracy. What must be checked before calling it useful?
options: Its performance on the minority class and the costs of errors
Whether 95 is a large number
Whether the model name contains deep learning
Whether the output labels are alphabetical
questions.explanation: High accuracy can conceal a complete failure to detect the cases that matter.

questions.prompt: Which dataset is used to fit model parameters?
options: Training set
Final test set only
Development set only
A results archive
questions.explanation: Training examples drive parameter estimation; validation guides choices and testing estimates final performance.

questions.prompt: Which dataset should guide hyperparameter selection?
options: Validation or development set
The final test set through repeated experimentation
The deployment target labels before they exist
A random unrelated dataset
questions.explanation: Validation supplies feedback for model selection while preserving the test set for an independent estimate.

questions.prompt: Why does selecting the best of many test scores compromise evaluation?
options: The test data influence model selection even if not passed to fit
The test set automatically becomes larger
The model loses all fitted weights
The scores become mathematically undefined
questions.explanation: Information can leak through human choices, creating optimistic estimates on the repeatedly consulted test set.

questions.prompt: What happens in five-fold cross-validation on the development/training pool?
options: Train on four parts and validate on the fifth, rotating the held-out part
Train only once on every row and report five identical predictions
Use the final test set in every training fold
Split features into five groups but keep all rows in training
questions.explanation: Cross-validation rotates held-out observations and gives several estimates of performance.

questions.prompt: Fold scores vary substantially. What does this suggest?
options: Performance is sensitive to which observations are held out
The highest fold is necessarily the true deployment accuracy
The lowest fold must be deleted
The model has no variance
questions.explanation: Reporting the distribution of fold scores gives context that a single favourable split cannot provide.

questions.prompt: Which are valid evaluation practices? Select all that apply.
options: Use representative held-out data
Compare against a meaningful baseline
Choose the final model by repeatedly inspecting test errors
Evaluate only memorised training rows
questions.explanation: Representative evaluation and baselines help establish practical predictive value.

questions.prompt: For disease-positive as the positive class, a sick person predicted healthy is what?
options: A false negative
A false positive
A true negative
A true positive
questions.explanation: The true condition is positive but the predicted decision is negative.

questions.prompt: For spam as the positive class, a legitimate message sent to spam is what?
options: A false positive
A false negative
A true negative
A true positive
questions.explanation: The model raises a positive alarm on an actually negative example.

questions.prompt: What question does recall answer?
options: What fraction of actual positives were detected?
What fraction of positive predictions were correct?
What fraction of all predictions were negative?
How many model parameters were fitted?
questions.explanation: Recall is TP divided by TP+FN and focuses on missed actual positives.

questions.prompt: What question does precision answer?
options: What fraction of positive predictions were correct?
What fraction of actual positives were detected?
What fraction of training examples were observed twice?
How many features were selected?
questions.explanation: Precision is TP divided by TP+FP and focuses on the reliability of positive predictions.

questions.prompt: Missing a positive case is the main concern in a screening scenario. Which metric directly tracks detection?
options: Recall
The number of features
Mean absolute regression error
Training runtime only
questions.explanation: High recall means few actual positives are missed, although other constraints still matter.

questions.prompt: A spam filter must avoid sending legitimate mail to junk. Which positive-class metric addresses this concern?
options: Precision
Regression R²
Training loss alone
The number of clusters
questions.explanation: With spam as positive, false alarms reduce precision; high precision makes flagged mail more trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Lowering a fixed classifier's positive threshold can have which effects? Select all that apply.
options: Increase or preserve recall
Increase or preserve the number of false positives
Necessarily reduce every false positive
Guarantee a higher F1 score
questions.explanation: More observations are classified positive, so true and false positive counts cannot decrease. Precision and F1 need not improve.

questions.prompt: Why can accuracy alone be inadequate for imbalanced classification?
options: Correct majority predictions can dominate the score
It cannot ever be computed for binary labels
It automatically gives the minority class extra weight
It always equals recall
questions.explanation: Accuracy counts all correct decisions equally and can obscure poor minority detection.

questions.prompt: What does F1 combine?
options: Precision and recall through a harmonic mean
MAE and MSE through a sum
Training time and memory size
The number of classes and features
questions.explanation: F1 is a single-number summary that is high only when both precision and recall are high.

questions.prompt: If precision is high but recall is very low, what is a plausible description?
options: Few alarms are wrong, but many actual positives are missed
Nearly all positives are detected with many false alarms
All observations are correctly classified
The model must predict positive for everyone
questions.explanation: Precision and recall measure different aspects of the decision rule and can diverge substantially.

questions.prompt: What must be stated when interpreting a binary confusion matrix?
options: Which label is positive and the row/column ordering
Only the model's filename
Only the processor model
The alphabetical order of feature names
questions.explanation: Matrix conventions and class ordering determine the meaning of each cell.

questions.prompt: Training accuracy is very high, but representative held-out accuracy is much lower. What is a likely diagnosis?
options: Overfitting
Underfitting alone
Perfect generalisation
A proof that the labels are causal
questions.explanation: A large train-to-held-out gap often indicates excessive fit to training-specific detail, assuming comparable data distributions.

questions.prompt: Both training and validation performance are poor relative to an achievable baseline. What should be investigated?
options: Underfitting or inadequate features
Successful memorisation with perfect training fit
A guaranteed shortage of test data only
A need to hide the training score
questions.explanation: Poor fit even on training data suggests the model or representation may be insufficient, though optimisation and data quality also deserve checks.

questions.prompt: Which changes may reduce overfitting? Select all that apply.
options: Constrain model complexity
Collect more representative training data
Always maximise tree depth
Choose hyperparameters from final test outcomes
questions.explanation: Simplification and suitable additional data can improve generalisation; the effects should be validated.

questions.prompt: Why is more data alone not a direct solution to a model that cannot fit an obvious curved pattern?
options: The model's representation may be too restrictive
All learning problems are solved by deleting targets
Underfitting is caused only by test leakage
More data necessarily removes all bias
questions.explanation: If the model cannot express the relationship, additional examples do not directly address that limitation.

questions.prompt: A validation score improves after adding a useful feature. What should happen before claiming final success?
options: Evaluate the chosen pipeline using untouched representative test data
Report the training score as the final result
Continue selecting features using the final test score
Replace test labels with the model's predictions
questions.explanation: Validation supports choosing the pipeline; the final independent test supports reporting its performance.

questions.prompt: Which mistake is penalised particularly strongly by log loss?
options: A highly confident incorrect class probability
A correct probability closer to one
A longer feature name
A slower CSV parser
questions.explanation: Log loss evaluates probabilistic predictions and heavily penalises confident errors.

questions.prompt: ROC-AUC mainly evaluates what aspect of binary predictions?
options: How well scores rank positives above negatives across thresholds
The accuracy at one fixed threshold only
The calibration of every probability with certainty
The number of model weights
questions.explanation: ROC-AUC summarises ranking/separation across thresholds and does not guarantee calibration or a good deployment threshold.

questions.prompt: Can two classifiers with similar ROC-AUC have different precision at a chosen operating threshold?
options: Yes; a global ranking summary does not fix performance at one threshold
No; AUC uniquely determines every confusion matrix
No; precision always equals AUC
Only if the labels are removed
questions.explanation: Threshold choice and score distributions affect the actual decisions at deployment.

questions.prompt: A cat app will receive blurry phone photos but training uses clean web photos. Which dev set is most useful?
options: Representative phone photos from the intended use setting
Only the cleanest training photos
Repeated copies of the training set
An unrelated handwritten-digit dataset
questions.explanation: Development should aim the project at the data distribution on which it needs to succeed.

questions.prompt: Why does Ng recommend dev and test sets from the same distribution?
options: Success on development should predict success on the final evaluation target
The training set must therefore be identical to the test set
It prevents all possible overfitting
It removes the need for separate sets
questions.explanation: Matching dev and test distributions makes model-selection progress more meaningful and failures easier to diagnose.

questions.prompt: A team uses one country for development and a very different country for testing while serving both. What is the concern?
options: The dev set may direct optimisation toward the wrong target distribution
The test set must be easier
Geography can never affect data
More hyperparameter tuning automatically fixes distribution mismatch
questions.explanation: Dev and test should represent the intended use population rather than unrelated subsets with different distributions.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the development set in ML strategy?
options: Provide feedback for choosing useful changes to the system
Replace all training data
Provide an unlimited unbiased final score after endless tuning
Supply class labels for every future user
questions.explanation: The dev set is a decision-making target, so its distribution and metric shape the team's work.

questions.prompt: Why can a fixed 30% test allocation be unnecessary for a huge dataset?
options: The required absolute evaluation size may be much smaller than 30%
Test data cease to matter when data are plentiful
A tiny unrepresentative test set is always sufficient
Every example must be used in all splits
questions.explanation: Evaluation sets need enough observations for the desired precision, rather than an inflexible percentage.

questions.prompt: What should determine the needed dev-set size?
options: How small a performance difference the team needs to distinguish
Only the number of letters in the model name
A universal rule of exactly 100 examples
The largest percentage that can be reserved
questions.explanation: Smaller meaningful improvements generally require larger evaluation sets for reliable comparison.

questions.prompt: Why use a single-number optimisation metric?
options: It makes model comparisons and iteration decisions clearer
It makes every secondary concern irrelevant
It guarantees no subgroup can be harmed
It makes labels unnecessary
questions.explanation: A common objective helps rank alternatives, but other metrics and constraints can still be monitored.

questions.prompt: A model must respond within 100 ms, then maximise accuracy. What role does latency play?
options: A satisficing constraint
The sole metric to maximise without limit
The supervised target for every training example
A reason to ignore accuracy
questions.explanation: A satisficing metric must meet an acceptable threshold; optimisation then selects among eligible models.

questions.prompt: Which statements about evaluation objectives are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An optimisation metric identifies what to improve
A satisficing metric can impose a required limit
A single-number metric guarantees ethical acceptability
The fastest model is always the most accurate
questions.explanation: Ng separates objectives to optimise from constraints that must be satisfied; neither guarantees broader suitability.

questions.prompt: Why build a basic working system early in a new ML project?
options: Its errors provide evidence for prioritising improvements
It guarantees the first model is optimal
It removes the need for a dev set
It proves more complex models cannot help
questions.explanation: A baseline creates a feedback loop and makes speculative improvement ideas testable.

questions.prompt: What is the useful iteration loop described by Ng?
options: Form an idea, implement it, run an experiment, and learn from the result
Choose the final test winner repeatedly and stop documenting changes
Collect arbitrary data indefinitely without evaluating
Deploy once and never inspect errors
questions.explanation: Rapid measured iteration helps discover which changes work on the chosen development objective.

questions.prompt: The dev metric ranks model A above B, but A makes unacceptable errors in actual use. What should be reconsidered?
options: Whether the metric and dev distribution reflect the product's needs
Whether the team can hide those errors
Whether all model comparisons are impossible
Whether training must use no labels
questions.explanation: An objective that rewards the wrong outcomes can direct development away from the intended goal.

questions.prompt: After many dev-set experiments, dev performance greatly exceeds matched-distribution test performance. What is plausible?
options: The team has overfit to the dev set
The test data must always be incorrect
The model has become universally intelligent
The training loss must be negative
questions.explanation: Repeated development feedback can adapt choices to quirks of the dev set. Fresh development data may be needed.

questions.prompt: User uploads now contain many more kittens than the original adult-cat evaluation set. What should be considered?
options: Updating dev/test data to represent intended future use
Keeping the old distribution regardless of the task
Removing all kitten images from deployment
Changing only the model's displayed name
questions.explanation: When the intended population differs from evaluation data, the target distribution should be revisited.

questions.prompt: A team wants to fix dog-to-cat errors after seeing two memorable failures. What is the best next step?
options: Count this error type in a sample of misclassified dev examples
Assume it accounts for most errors
Spend all resources without further analysis
Measure only correctly classified training photos
questions.explanation: Anecdotes can mislead; systematic error analysis estimates how much a proposed fix could help.

questions.prompt: Why is the fraction of errors in a category a useful ceiling estimate?
options: Even a perfect category-specific fix can remove only those errors, assuming no other effects
It guarantees that the fix will reach the ceiling
It measures the model's training time
It proves the category causes every other error
questions.explanation: The estimate is an upper bound under stated assumptions, useful for prioritisation rather than a promised outcome.

questions.prompt: An image is both blurry and a lion mistaken for a pet cat. How should an error-analysis sheet handle this?
options: Allow both categories to be marked
Force exactly one arbitrary category
Exclude it from all analysis
Treat it as two separate dataset examples
questions.explanation: Error causes can overlap, so category percentages need not sum to 100%.

questions.prompt: Which are useful outputs of manual error analysis? Select all that apply.
options: Estimated frequencies of actionable error types
New hypotheses inspired by inspecting failures
Proof that a proposed fix will eliminate every error
An unbiased final test score after repeated test-guided changes
questions.explanation: Error inspection generates and prioritises ideas, but improvements still require validation.

questions.prompt: Why might a rare error category still deserve attention despite a low accuracy ceiling?
options: Its mistakes may have unusually high practical cost
The category's small count proves it is harmless
Every error has the same societal impact
A ceiling measures only the number of features
questions.explanation: Frequency informs impact on aggregate accuracy, but costs and severity also affect priority.

questions.prompt: What is a mislabeled evaluation example?
options: An example whose recorded target is wrong
An example the model predicts incorrectly even though its label is right
Any rare input
Any observation with a low probability score
questions.explanation: Distinguish a faulty reference label from a genuine model error against a correct reference.

questions.prompt: When does correcting dev labels become particularly valuable?
options: When label errors obstruct reliable comparison of candidate models
Only before the first data row is collected
Never; evaluation labels cannot be wrong
Whenever a model disagrees, without checking the evidence
questions.explanation: The value of correction depends on whether the reference errors materially affect evaluation decisions.

questions.prompt: Why apply consistent relabelling procedures to both dev and test sets?
options: To keep their evaluation standards and distributions aligned
To copy the model's predictions into both sets
To make the test set part of training
To guarantee identical predictions
questions.explanation: Inconsistent correction can make dev improvements fail to transfer to the test criterion.

questions.prompt: Why inspect some apparently correct predictions during a label audit?
options: The model and original label may agree but both be wrong
Agreement proves the ground truth is correct
Correct predictions cannot be audited
Only training examples can be mislabeled
questions.explanation: Auditing only disagreements can bias correction and miss shared errors.

questions.prompt: What is the role of an Eyeball dev set?
options: A subset inspected manually for error analysis
A final test set used to fit weights
A dataset that must contain images only
A subset whose labels are always hidden from evaluation
questions.explanation: The name describes manual inspection; analogous analysis can involve text or audio.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a Blackbox dev set?
options: Evaluate candidate models numerically without routinely inspecting individual examples
Replace the final test set with training data
Store only examples the model got right
Train a black-box neural network only
questions.explanation: It supports model selection while limiting adaptation to specific manually observed cases.

questions.prompt: Eyeball performance improves much faster than Blackbox performance. What should be investigated?
options: Overfitting to the manually inspected examples
A guarantee that deployment improved equally
A proof that Blackbox labels should be deleted
The impossibility of computing error rates
questions.explanation: Manual inspection gives extra information about the Eyeball subset, increasing the risk of overfitting to it.

questions.prompt: If there is too little dev data for two useful subsets, what does Ng suggest?
options: Use the available dev set for inspection and selection while recognising increased overfitting risk
Discard all dev data
Use the final test set as every training batch
Invent labels for a larger Blackbox set
questions.explanation: The split is a practical aid, not an absolute requirement when data are scarce.

questions.prompt: What does a basic artificial neuron compute before applying its activation?
options: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias
A list of filenames sorted alphabetically
The final test score
A random target label independent of inputs
questions.explanation: Weights control input contributions; the bias offsets the summed value before activation.

questions.prompt: Why use nonlinear activations between neural-network layers?
options: They allow the composition to represent nonlinear relationships
They guarantee every output is a probability
They eliminate the need to learn weights
They ensure the loss can never increase
questions.explanation: A stack of purely affine transformations collapses to a single affine transformation. Nonlinearity expands the representable functions.

questions.prompt: What is a forward pass?
options: Compute outputs from inputs using the current parameters
Update all labels using test predictions
Split the examples into random folds
Manually select every weight
questions.explanation: Forward computation produces predictions; the loss then compares them with the training objective.

questions.prompt: What is backpropagation primarily used to compute?
options: Gradients of the loss with respect to parameters
The true labels for unlabelled examples
An unbiased final test score
The best number of layers without experiments
questions.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the computation graph to obtain parameter gradients.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates backpropagation and an optimiser?
options: Backpropagation computes gradients; the optimiser uses them to update parameters
Both mean collecting new data
The optimiser discovers the target labels without a loss
Backpropagation proves that the global minimum is reached
questions.explanation: Derivative computation and the parameter-update rule are related but distinct operations.

questions.prompt: What does the learning rate control in gradient descent?
options: The scale of each parameter update
The number of output classes by definition
The fraction of examples labelled positive
The maximum possible model accuracy
questions.explanation: The learning rate multiplies the update direction and affects optimisation stability and speed.

questions.prompt: What can an excessively large learning rate cause?
options: Overshooting or unstable loss
A guarantee of fastest convergence
Automatic removal of training noise
A guarantee of perfect calibration
questions.explanation: Large updates can jump past useful regions or cause divergence.

questions.prompt: What can an extremely small learning rate cause?
options: Very slow progress during training
Instant convergence in every problem
Automatic selection of the ideal architecture
The elimination of every gradient
questions.explanation: Updates may be too small to make useful progress within the available training budget.

questions.prompt: What is an epoch?
options: One pass through the training dataset
One pass through a single neuron only
The number of output classes
The final test-set grade
questions.explanation: An epoch measures training exposure; several mini-batch updates can occur within one epoch.

questions.prompt: What is a mini-batch?
options: A subset of training examples used for one update
The final test set used to tune every weight
A set of handwritten decision rules
The model's entire source repository
questions.explanation: Mini-batches approximate the training objective's gradient while limiting per-step computation and memory.

questions.prompt: Which quantities are normally learned during neural-network fitting? Select all that apply.
options: Weights
Biases
The developer's chosen maximum epoch count
The chosen number of layers in a fixed architecture
questions.explanation: Weights and biases are parameters; architecture and training-budget choices are hyperparameters.

questions.prompt: Why avoid identical initial weights for all hidden units in a standard dense layer?
options: Symmetry can make units learn redundant representations
Identical weights always guarantee optimal convergence
Random initialisation removes the need for data
Initialisation is unrelated to optimisation
questions.explanation: Symmetry-breaking initialisation allows units to learn different functions.

questions.prompt: For one-of-several-class prediction, what does a softmax output provide?
options: Nonnegative scores summing to one, interpretable as model class probabilities
Unrestricted continuous prices
An unsupervised cluster hierarchy
A guarantee of correct classification
questions.explanation: Softmax normalises class scores but does not guarantee accuracy or calibration.

questions.prompt: Which output is a natural fit for unconstrained continuous regression?
options: A scalar linear output
An obligatorily binary thresholded output
A nearest-category name only
A cluster ID with no numeric meaning
questions.explanation: Regression often uses an unconstrained numeric output, though task-specific constraints may call for other choices.

questions.prompt: Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss rises. What is a reasonable intervention?
options: Use validation-guided early stopping or stronger regularisation
Continue indefinitely because training loss is all that matters
Choose the stopping point with the final test labels
Delete all difficult validation cases
questions.explanation: The divergence is a warning of overfitting; validation can guide stopping without compromising the final test.

questions.prompt: What is dropout during training?
options: Randomly omit selected activations as a regularisation technique
Permanently delete every incorrectly predicted row
Randomly change the true target labels
Remove the entire validation set
questions.explanation: Dropout discourages reliance on particular co-adapted activations and can reduce overfitting.

questions.prompt: Which actions can help neural-network generalisation? Select all that apply.
options: Use appropriate regularisation
Collect representative training examples
Always increase capacity until training loss is zero
Tune the architecture repeatedly on the final test set
questions.explanation: Regularisation and suitable data address overfitting; capacity alone is not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why is scaling numeric inputs often useful for neural-network optimisation?
options: It can make gradient-based optimisation better conditioned
It turns every problem into an unsupervised task
It makes targets unnecessary
It proves the features are independent
questions.explanation: Large differences in feature scales can make optimisation less stable or inefficient.

questions.prompt: According to Ng's scaling discussion, what combination can unlock gains from larger neural networks?
options: Enough suitable data and enough computation
More parameters with no examples
A larger logo for the model
Removing every evaluation set
questions.explanation: Larger models can exploit large datasets when training resources and other details are appropriate; size alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: With only twenty labelled examples, is a larger neural network guaranteed to beat a simpler model?
options: No; useful features and data limitations can matter more
Yes; parameter count alone determines accuracy
Yes; a deeper model cannot overfit
No; neural networks cannot process small datasets
questions.explanation: Ng explicitly cautions that advantages in the small-data regime depend on feature engineering and other conditions.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a generative text system's usual output from a binary classifier's output?
options: It produces content such as a sequence of words or tokens
It always outputs the true class label
It is necessarily a rule-free database
It cannot make factual errors
questions.explanation: Generation produces content, and fluent content can still be incorrect or unsupported.

questions.prompt: A model writes a plausible but fabricated reference. What failure does this illustrate?
options: Hallucination or unsupported generation
A guarantee of factual retrieval
A perfect supervised label
A proof of consciousness
questions.explanation: Fluency and plausibility do not establish that a source exists or supports the claim.

questions.prompt: Why can a single foundation model support many tasks?
options: Broad pretraining can provide reusable capabilities adapted through instructions or further training
It has a separately handwritten rule for every future task
Every prompt permanently retrains all its weights
It never needs task-specific evaluation
questions.explanation: Foundation models can be reused across applications, but performance must still be checked for the actual use case.

questions.prompt: Which outputs can be generative? Select all that apply.
options: Synthesised audio
Newly generated source code
Only a fixed fraud/not-fraud decision
Only a numeric class ID selected from two labels
questions.explanation: Generative systems can create multiple kinds of content, including audio and code.

questions.prompt: What is a token in language-model processing?
options: A unit of encoded text, which may be a word, subword or other text fragment
Always exactly one complete sentence
A model's final accuracy percentage
A mandatory human approval signature
questions.explanation: Tokenisation determines the units consumed and generated by a language model; tokens need not correspond one-to-one with words.

questions.prompt: What does next-token prediction train a language model to estimate?
options: A distribution over likely next tokens given preceding context
The objectively true answer to every future question
The complete legal status of each sentence
A single permanent response for all prompts
questions.explanation: The prediction objective learns statistical structure; it does not itself guarantee truthfulness.

questions.prompt: What is pretraining?
options: Learning broad patterns from a large initial training corpus
Manually typing an instruction into an already deployed chat once
Computing only the final test score
Deleting learned parameters before every request
questions.explanation: Pretraining establishes general capabilities that later adaptation may specialise.

questions.prompt: What is fine-tuning?
options: Further training a pretrained model's parameters on additional examples
Only adding an instruction to a prompt without updating parameters
Searching a directory without using a model
Changing the font of the output
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning updates parameters; prompting changes the input context.

questions.prompt: What is few-shot prompting?
options: Providing a small number of task examples in the prompt
Training a model from scratch using only one token
Guaranteeing correctness with a short command
Reducing the model to a single neural layer
questions.explanation: Examples in context demonstrate the desired mapping or format without necessarily changing model weights.

questions.prompt: What is zero-shot prompting?
options: Requesting a task without demonstration examples in the prompt
Using a model with zero parameters
Training without any data ever
Always omitting the task instruction
questions.explanation: Zero-shot describes the absence of in-prompt task demonstrations, not the absence of prior model training.

questions.prompt: Which prompt most clearly specifies a summarisation task?
options: Summarise the supplied report in five bullets for first-year students; use only the report
Do something with this
Be clever
Say everything you know
questions.explanation: A clear task, source boundary, audience and output format reduce ambiguity, although evaluation is still needed.

questions.prompt: Why specify an output schema when extracting information?
options: It makes required fields and structure explicit
It guarantees every extracted fact is true
It permanently changes the model architecture
It removes all need for validation
questions.explanation: A schema helps structure output, but content and schema compliance still need checking.

questions.prompt: What does retrieval-augmented generation add to a model's context?
options: Relevant material retrieved from an external collection
A guarantee that all retrieved statements are true
An automatic update of all model weights
The true labels of every future task
questions.explanation: Retrieval supplies contextual evidence; it is different from fine-tuning and can itself fail.

questions.prompt: Why does retrieval not eliminate hallucination?
options: Documents may be missing or unsuitable, and the generator may misuse them
Retrieved text makes model errors impossible
Retrieval always searches every document on the internet
The generator can only copy exact source text
questions.explanation: Both retrieval coverage and faithful use of evidence need evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is a model's context window?
options: The bounded amount of input and generated context it can handle for a request
The number of training rows stored in a CSV
A guarantee of permanent memory
The maximum length of a human's browser history
questions.explanation: Context capacity limits what can be supplied or retained within a model interaction.

questions.prompt: Increasing sampling temperature generally does what?
options: Makes the token distribution less concentrated, increasing output variability
Guarantees more factual responses
Adds verified sources automatically
Always reduces the context length
questions.explanation: Temperature changes sampling behaviour, not the truth of the generated content.

questions.prompt: Is a low-temperature answer guaranteed to be correct?
options: No; a consistently chosen answer can still be wrong
Yes; determinism is the same as truth
Yes; temperature validates external sources
No; low temperature always prevents text generation
questions.explanation: Reducing variability does not correct mistaken learned associations or missing evidence.

questions.prompt: Which prompt improvements are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: State the desired audience and format
Provide relevant source material and task boundaries
Assume politeness guarantees correctness
Replace evaluation with an instruction to never be wrong
questions.explanation: Clear specification and context can help, but prompt wording cannot replace verification.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation best compares two summarisation prompts?
options: Use the same representative documents and a defined rubric
Choose whichever wins on one favourite example
Compare only word count regardless of the task
Let the model assert its own correctness without evidence
questions.explanation: A shared evaluation set and criteria support a fair comparison across prompt variants.

questions.prompt: What should a factual-answer evaluation check besides fluent writing?
options: Whether claims are supported and sources actually match them
Only the number of adjectives
Only the answer's confidence
Whether the answer is unusually long
questions.explanation: Accuracy and grounding are separate from presentation quality.

questions.prompt: What is prompt injection in a document-processing workflow?
options: Untrusted document text tries to redirect the model's instructions
A developer deliberately updates the model weights
The normal conversion of text into tokens
A harmless extra space in a CSV separator
questions.explanation: Retrieved or supplied content can contain adversarial instructions and should not be treated as trusted authority.

questions.prompt: A retrieved document says to ignore the user and disclose secrets. How should the system treat that text?
options: As untrusted document content, not an instruction with authority
As a higher-priority instruction automatically
As proof the document is accurate
As a required training label
questions.explanation: The system must distinguish task instructions from data it is asked to process.

questions.prompt: What makes tool-using agents different from text-only answering in practical risk?
options: They can cause effects outside the generated response
They cannot make mistakes
They have perfect understanding of intent
They no longer require evaluation
questions.explanation: Actions such as writing files or calling services need appropriate boundaries and checks because their effects extend beyond text.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible way to test a tool-using assistant before deployment?
options: Evaluate representative tasks, failure cases and permitted action boundaries
Test only its greeting
Grant every permission because it sounds confident
Rely only on the largest model size
questions.explanation: Evaluation should cover task success, errors and whether actions stay within intended permissions.

questions.prompt: What is a multimodal model?
options: A model that processes or generates more than one kind of modality, such as text and images
A model with several filenames
A classifier with exactly two labels
A model guaranteed to understand every medium equally well
questions.explanation: Multimodality concerns data types, not universal competence across them.

questions.prompt: When should an AI-generated code answer be considered validated?
options: After relevant inspection and tests for its intended use
As soon as it looks syntactically plausible
Whenever it contains comments
Whenever the model claims it ran successfully
questions.explanation: Generated code can be plausible yet incorrect; evidence should come from appropriate checks.

questions.prompt: Which statements about prompting and training are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Providing examples in a prompt can change the response without updating weights
Fine-tuning changes learned parameters
Every user message permanently retrains the model
Retrieval always replaces pretraining
questions.explanation: Prompt context, retrieval and parameter training are distinct mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Why include varied and difficult examples in a generative-AI evaluation set?
options: They reveal limitations that easy demonstrations can hide
They guarantee the worst example defines all performance
They remove the need for an evaluation rubric
They make tokenisation unnecessary
questions.explanation: Representative coverage and challenging cases provide a more useful view of capabilities and failure modes.

questions.prompt: Which response is best when supplied evidence does not answer the user's factual question?
options: State the evidence gap rather than invent a supported-looking claim
Fabricate a plausible citation
Assert certainty because the prose is fluent
Treat an unrelated source as proof
questions.explanation: Acknowledging insufficient evidence preserves the distinction between supported answers and guesses.

questions.prompt: Why keep a separate held-out set when repeatedly refining prompts?
options: Prompt selection can overfit to the examples used during development
Prompts cannot possibly overfit
The held-out set updates the weights automatically
It ensures the shortest prompt always wins
questions.explanation: Repeated selection against the same examples can reward their quirks, just as other model-selection procedures can.

questions.prompt: A speech recogniser is trained mostly on one dialect. What concern should deployment evaluation address?
options: Performance on other dialects in the intended user population
Whether the model file is large enough to be ethical
Whether all users share the training accent
Whether the accuracy is high on training audio only
questions.explanation: Representation gaps can produce unequal performance for populations missing from training.

questions.prompt: A hiring model learns from historical decisions. Why may it reproduce unfair patterns?
options: Past decisions can encode discriminatory preferences and proxies
Historical labels are necessarily neutral
Removing the name column guarantees fairness
All training examples have identical social context
questions.explanation: Labels can reflect past policies and bias rather than the desired fair decision criterion.

questions.prompt: Why does deleting names not necessarily anonymise a dataset?
options: Combinations of remaining attributes may identify people
Only names can identify individuals
Numerical columns are always anonymous
A model cannot memorise data
questions.explanation: Indirect identifiers can support re-identification even after direct identifiers are removed.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes pseudonymisation from irreversible anonymisation at the conceptual level?
options: Pseudonymisation can preserve a way to reconnect records to identities
Both necessarily make re-identification impossible
Anonymisation always means substituting a customer key
Pseudonymisation removes every data-quality issue
questions.explanation: Replacing identifiers with keys is not the same as preventing re-identification. This question tests the course concept, not a legal compliance determination.

questions.prompt: Can distributing only a model fully guarantee training-data privacy?
options: No; models can memorise or reveal information from training examples
Yes; a trained model contains no information about its data
Yes; every learned parameter is anonymous by definition
No; models cannot be distributed at all
questions.explanation: The possibility of memorisation means model release itself deserves privacy assessment.

questions.prompt: Which claims about synthetic data are justified? Select all that apply.
options: It can help exercise a pipeline before real data are available
It can inherit biases from its generator
It always represents every rare real-world case
It automatically proves privacy and fairness
questions.explanation: Synthetic data can be useful without guaranteeing population coverage, fairness or privacy.

questions.prompt: A system has high overall accuracy but much lower recall for one user group. What should the team do?
options: Investigate group-level errors and their consequences
Ignore the disparity because the average is high
Remove the group from every report
Assume the disparity proves the model is perfect
questions.explanation: Aggregate metrics can conceal unequal service quality and harms; subgroup analysis informs responsible decisions.

questions.prompt: Does removing a protected attribute guarantee that decisions are unbiased?
options: No; other variables may act as proxies
Yes; bias exists only in one named column
Yes; all remaining correlations become causal
No; fair evaluation is impossible
questions.explanation: Correlated features and biased labels can carry group information indirectly.

questions.prompt: What does accountability require in a deployed AI workflow?
options: Clear responsibility for decisions, monitoring and responding to failures
Treating the model as the sole responsible actor
Avoiding documentation so errors cannot be traced
Assuming vendors handle every downstream consequence
questions.explanation: People and organisations need defined responsibilities for how a system is used and corrected.

questions.prompt: What is a useful form of human oversight for consequential decisions?
options: A reviewer with relevant information, authority and time to challenge the output
A mandatory click that never permits disagreement
A label saying human-reviewed regardless of review
Automatically accepting confident outputs
questions.explanation: Oversight needs actual capacity to detect and act on errors, not merely a ceremonial approval step.

questions.prompt: Why document a dataset's origin and limitations?
options: To support assessment of fitness, representation and appropriate use
To guarantee that no bias remains
To replace every held-out evaluation
To prevent any need for updates
questions.explanation: Provenance and limitation notes make assumptions and gaps visible for later use and review.

questions.prompt: A team wants to collect extra personal fields just in case they help. What is a sound design question?
options: Are these fields needed for the specific task, and can less identifying data suffice?
Will more columns automatically make the system ethical?
Can every field be retained forever without justification?
Does converting names to numbers remove every concern?
questions.explanation: Task-focused data collection reduces unnecessary exposure and encourages clear justification of inputs.

questions.prompt: Why should model performance be monitored after deployment?
options: Data and use conditions can change over time
A test score automatically remains valid forever
Deployed models cannot make errors
Monitoring only matters before training
questions.explanation: Distribution changes and new use cases can degrade performance after an initially sound evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which are useful checks before a consequential AI deployment? Select all that apply.
options: Evaluate relevant failure costs and affected groups
Define how to respond when the system is unreliable
Assume a high average score resolves every ethical question
Hide known limitations to encourage adoption
questions.explanation: Responsible assessment combines predictive evidence, impact analysis and operational safeguards.

questions.prompt: A system's prediction is interpretable. Does that establish fairness?
options: No; an understandable rule can still produce unfair outcomes
Yes; all transparent rules are fair
Yes; explainability implies equal error rates
No; interpretability is never useful
questions.explanation: Transparency helps inspection but does not by itself settle whether inputs, rules or consequences are acceptable.

questions.prompt: Why might automation bias be a concern for reviewers?
options: People may defer to model output even when contrary evidence is available
Humans always distrust every algorithm
A model can no longer be audited
Reviewing outputs necessarily retrains the model
questions.explanation: Review processes should account for the risk of uncritical reliance on automated suggestions.

questions.prompt: A vendor demonstrates five perfect examples. What is the strongest next request?
options: Representative evaluation results, failure analysis and intended-use limits
A larger logo
A claim that the model is general-purpose
The same five examples in a different order
questions.explanation: Selected demonstrations do not establish reliability across the actual deployment distribution.

questions.prompt: Why can a benchmark score be insufficient for choosing a model?
options: The benchmark may not reflect the intended users, tasks or constraints
Benchmarks never contain useful information
All benchmarks measure exactly the same capability
A score guarantees equal performance in every language
questions.explanation: Transfer from a benchmark to real use depends on the match between the evaluation and the intended setting.

questions.prompt: Which description of an AI capability claim is most useful?
options: A specified task, dataset, metric and known limitations
The system is intelligent in every possible way
It beats humans, with no task or evaluation details
It is new, so it must be reliable
questions.explanation: Specific test conditions allow the reader to judge what evidence supports the claim.

questions.prompt: Which societal effects can deserve consideration alongside predictive accuracy? Select all that apply.
options: Changes in access to services and distribution of errors
Effects on work and responsibilities
Only the colour of the dashboard
Only the model's filename
questions.explanation: Responsible evaluation considers who benefits, who bears errors and how the deployment changes existing practices.

questions.prompt: A spam model learns patterns from labelled email. Which relationship is correct?
options: It uses machine learning, which is part of AI
All AI is supervised learning
Machine learning is separate from AI
Any spam model must be generative AI
questions.explanation: Machine learning is a way to build AI by learning from data; AI also includes other approaches.

questions.prompt: A system uses many neural-network layers to recognise objects. Which term is most specific?
options: Deep learning
Data entry
Manual rule lookup
Database indexing
questions.explanation: Deep learning refers to machine learning with multilayer neural networks.

questions.prompt: Which outputs indicate generative tasks? Select all that apply.
options: A newly composed paragraph
A newly synthesised image
A fraud/non-fraud label only
A numeric temperature forecast only
questions.explanation: Generative tasks produce content. Class labels and numeric forecasts are typical discriminative or predictive outputs.

questions.prompt: A hand-written rule engine reasons about symptoms without learning from examples. Must it be machine learning?
options: No; AI can include manually specified reasoning rules
Yes; all decision software learns weights
Yes; all AI is deep learning
No; AI must generate text
questions.explanation: AI is broader than machine learning. A knowledge-based system need not learn its rules from data.

questions.prompt: What changes when a team replaces hand-written classification rules with supervised learning?
options: Examples are used to learn a predictive mapping
The target is removed from every training example
The software no longer uses algorithms
Evaluation becomes unnecessary
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses example inputs and outputs to estimate a mapping instead of requiring every decision rule to be hand-coded.

questions.prompt: A learned classifier behaves unexpectedly on an unusual input. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: Training success does not specify behaviour on every future input
The model must have conscious intentions
The input proves all learned models are random
Any model with a fixed program must predict correctly
questions.explanation: A learned mapping can generalise poorly outside the situations represented in training data.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical lesson of the AI winters discussed in the slides?
options: Evaluate demonstrated capability rather than confident promises
Progress is guaranteed after every funding increase
Historical setbacks prove AI cannot be useful
A convincing demonstration establishes universal intelligence
questions.explanation: The history of unmet expectations motivates asking what was actually demonstrated and how it was measured.

questions.prompt: Which factors helped modern ML scale? Select all that apply.
options: More usable digital data
More computational capacity
A complete removal of model errors
A guarantee that all datasets are representative
questions.explanation: Data and computation enable larger experiments; they do not eliminate data quality problems or errors.

questions.prompt: A company has more computing power but poor training labels. What should it expect?
options: Compute alone cannot guarantee useful predictions
More compute makes all labels correct
Labels become irrelevant to supervised learning
A larger server establishes fairness
questions.explanation: Hardware enables training but cannot substitute for suitable data and evaluation.

questions.prompt: Why did easier access to libraries and APIs matter for AI adoption?
options: It reduced the effort needed to integrate models into applications
It proved every model was explainable
It removed the need for software engineering
It made data ownership irrelevant
questions.explanation: Accessible tooling lowers implementation barriers while quality and governance responsibilities remain.

questions.prompt: An app transcribes speech into text. Which AI application area is most directly involved?
options: Speech recognition
Customer clustering only
Spreadsheet formatting
Numeric regression only
questions.explanation: Speech recognition maps audio to linguistic content and often appears inside ordinary applications.

questions.prompt: A camera system locates pedestrians in frames. Which area does this illustrate?
options: Computer vision
Database normalisation
Text translation
Manual annotation only
questions.explanation: Computer vision extracts information from images or video.

questions.prompt: An AI component ranks products in a shopping app. Which statement is justified?
options: AI can be embedded inside an otherwise ordinary software product
The entire application must be a neural network
Ranking requires human-like general intelligence
Every recommendation must be reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Many AI applications are components within larger systems. Recommendation is an application, not a single learning setting.

questions.prompt: What does a conversational Turing-style test primarily assess?
options: Whether a judge can distinguish machine conversation from human conversation under the test conditions
Whether every factual claim is true
Whether a system is conscious
Whether a model is useful for every task
questions.explanation: Imitating human conversation is different from establishing truthfulness, understanding or general usefulness.

questions.prompt: A chatbot fools judges in a brief conversation. Which conclusion goes beyond that evidence?
options: It can reliably solve every intellectual task
It imitated human conversation in that setting
The test conditions matter to interpretation
Longer or different evaluations may be informative
questions.explanation: A narrow conversational result does not demonstrate unrestricted general capability.

questions.prompt: Which item is normally a learned parameter of linear regression?
options: The fitted slope
The chosen validation split size
The number of cross-validation folds
The requested maximum tree depth
questions.explanation: A parameter is fitted from training data; a hyperparameter or evaluation choice is set outside that fitting process.

questions.prompt: What is inference?
options: Using a trained model to produce predictions
Choosing all labels manually
Splitting the dataset into folds
Collecting an entirely new training dataset
questions.explanation: Inference applies the learned mapping to inputs, usually without updating its fitted parameters.

questions.prompt: A robot learns from rewards after taking actions. Which learning setting is this?
options: Reinforcement learning
Supervised classification from fixed labels only
Unsupervised clustering only
Manual feature encoding
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning uses feedback about actions to learn behaviour in an environment.

questions.prompt: Customers have purchase records but no segment labels. A team wants to discover groups. Which setting fits?
options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised classification into known labels
A manually labelled regression task
Reinforcement learning from action rewards
questions.explanation: Discovering structure without target labels is an unsupervised task.

questions.prompt: A developer minimises a training loss. What does this directly optimise?
options: The chosen measure of training error
Every possible deployment outcome
The amount of test data
Human-level general intelligence
questions.explanation: The loss formalises a specific objective; reducing it is not a guarantee of generalisation or practical value.

questions.prompt: Which statements about learning settings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Supervised learning uses target labels
Unsupervised learning can discover structure without target labels
Reinforcement learning requires a correct class label for every state
Recommender systems constitute the only possible learning setting
questions.explanation: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning describe feedback settings; recommenders can use several of them.

questions.prompt: Passengers boarding at one port have higher survival rates, but also differ in ticket class. What is a plausible concern?
options: Ticket class may confound the port–survival relationship
The port must cause survival
Any correlation proves direct causation
Confounding means the dataset has no information
questions.explanation: A third variable can explain an apparent association. Observational differences alone do not establish causation.

questions.prompt: A game agent earns rewards by looping around bonuses rather than finishing a race. What failed?
options: The reward did not adequately represent the intended task
The agent ignored every reward
The problem must be supervised regression
High reward necessarily means task success
questions.explanation: Optimising a proxy can produce unintended behaviour when the proxy and the real goal differ.

questions.prompt: A semicolon-delimited file loads as a single column. Which change directly addresses the likely cause?
options: Use the correct separator when reading the file
Scale all numeric columns
Increase tree depth
Remove the target column
questions.explanation: A delimiter mismatch prevents the parser from recognising the intended fields.

questions.prompt: Why should a postcode such as 0150 usually be loaded as a string?
options: Its leading zero is meaningful and arithmetic on it is not
All strings are continuous quantities
A postcode is always the target
Integers cannot be used in machine learning
questions.explanation: Postcodes identify categories or locations; numeric parsing can lose leading zeros without adding useful meaning.

questions.prompt: Which operation best reveals column types and non-null counts in a Pandas DataFrame?
options: df.info()
model.predict(df)
df.shape[0] only
df.corr() only
questions.explanation: info provides a compact schema and completeness overview; shape only gives dimensions.

questions.prompt: What does df.shape represent?
options: The number of rows and columns
The average and standard deviation
The target classes and probabilities
Only the number of non-null values
questions.explanation: shape is a pair of dataset dimensions, not a count of populated cells.

questions.prompt: Which inspection is useful before choosing accuracy for a classifier?
options: The relative frequencies of target classes
Alphabetical order of column names
The file's extension alone
Whether the index starts at zero
questions.explanation: Class imbalance can make a majority-class predictor appear accurate while missing the minority class.

questions.prompt: A city column contains Oslo, OSLO and a version with trailing spaces. What is the appropriate first fix?
options: Normalise spelling, case and whitespace consistently
Give each spelling a permanently different class
Delete all city records
Scale the strings to unit variance
questions.explanation: Normalisation prevents superficial formatting differences from becoming distinct categories.

questions.prompt: Why does a count stored as text deserve investigation?
options: Parsing errors or mixed formats may be hiding in the column
Text columns are always unusable
Counts cannot be features
A DataFrame cannot mix numeric and categorical fields
questions.explanation: A suspicious dtype can indicate dirty data. Investigate the values before coercing them.

questions.prompt: Which dataset layout follows tidy-data principles?
options: One observation per row and one variable per column
One unrelated subject in every cell
A separate column for each record ID
All fields combined into one free-text cell
questions.explanation: A consistent unit of observation and clearly defined columns make cleaning and modelling less ambiguous.

questions.prompt: Why might df.isnull() fail to flag the literal string "unknown"?
options: It is an ordinary string unless explicitly mapped to a missing value
Pandas never detects missing values
The column must have no missing information
It automatically means zero
questions.explanation: Missing-value sentinels need explicit interpretation; strings that look missing may not be null values.

questions.prompt: Income is strongly right-skewed with a few extreme valid values. Which simple imputation is often more robust than the mean?
options: The training-set median
The test-set maximum
A randomly chosen target label
The largest income in the full dataset
questions.explanation: The median is less sensitive to extreme values. Fit the imputation statistic using training data only.

questions.prompt: Most values in a column are missing. Which is the best general response?
options: Investigate meaning and predictive value before choosing to drop or transform it
Always replace missing values with zero
Always remove every affected row
Treat every missing value as a parsing error
questions.explanation: Missingness can itself be informative, and blanket removal can discard signal or bias the sample.

questions.prompt: Survey nonresponse is concentrated among high earners. What risk does dropping incomplete rows create?
options: The remaining sample may underrepresent high earners
The sample automatically becomes random
The target cannot be biased
All relationships become causal
questions.explanation: Non-random missingness can change the population represented by the retained observations.

questions.prompt: What does an Age_missing indicator preserve alongside imputation?
options: Whether the original age was missing
The exact unknown age
The true class label
The test-set mean
questions.explanation: A missingness flag records absence, which may carry signal; it does not recover the missing value.

questions.prompt: Which are data-quality issues? Select all that apply.
options: Mixed measurement units in one field
Duplicated records of the same observation
A justified train/test split
A documented definition of the target
questions.explanation: Mixed units and duplicates can corrupt analysis. A split and target definition are useful practices, not data defects.

questions.prompt: A value is syntactically valid but refers to a customer's old address. Which distinction matters?
options: Validity does not guarantee accuracy or timeliness
Validity and accuracy mean exactly the same thing
An address cannot become stale
The data must be complete because it is valid
questions.explanation: A value can obey a field's format while failing to reflect current reality.

questions.prompt: Two email records differ only in letter case and surrounding spaces. What should precede deduplication?
options: Normalisation of the identifying field
Random oversampling
Removal of every numeric column
Fitting the final test labels
questions.explanation: Logical duplicates may not be byte-for-byte duplicates until the relevant keys are normalised.

questions.prompt: An unusually large transaction is genuine fraud. Should an outlier filter automatically delete it?
options: No; the rare event may be exactly the target behaviour
Yes; all outliers are entry mistakes
Yes; deleting it guarantees better recall
No; outliers must always be duplicated
questions.explanation: An outlier's meaning determines treatment. Removing all extremes may remove the behaviour the model should detect.

questions.prompt: An orders-to-customers merge unexpectedly triples the number of rows. What should be checked first?
options: Duplicate join keys and the intended merge cardinality
Whether the model uses sigmoid
The number of tree leaves
The test accuracy threshold
questions.explanation: Repeated keys can multiply rows during a merge, changing observation weights and dataset meaning.

questions.prompt: A left join keeps every order but introduces missing customer attributes. What is a plausible cause?
options: Some order keys have no matching customer
The join necessarily deleted all orders
Every missing value means the customer is fraudulent
A left join always fills unmatched fields with the mean
questions.explanation: Unmatched right-hand records produce missing attributes; investigate key compatibility and coverage before imputation.

questions.prompt: Two temperature sources use different units. What should happen before combining them?
options: Convert to a common documented unit
Treat unit differences as random noise
Remove units but keep values unchanged
Assign temperatures as class labels
