questions.explanation: Numerically plausible values can still be incompatible. Consistent units are essential for meaningful modelling.

questions.prompt: Why can encoding Oslo=0, Bergen=1, Trondheim=2 mislead a linear model?
options: It introduces an arbitrary order and spacing between nominal categories
It guarantees a fair model
It removes every category distinction
It prevents fitting coefficients
questions.explanation: Nominal categories do not have a natural numeric distance; one-hot encoding avoids imposing one.

questions.prompt: When is ordinal encoding appropriate?
options: For categories with a meaningful order that the model should use
For any arbitrary customer ID
Only for continuous temperatures
Whenever alphabetical order is available
questions.explanation: Ordinal encoding represents a genuine ranking, unlike an arbitrary numbering of nominal categories.

questions.prompt: Age ranges over tens and income over millions. Why can unscaled KNN be distorted?
options: Income differences can dominate distance calculations
KNN ignores all numerical features
Scaling turns classification into regression
Age becomes the target automatically
questions.explanation: Distance-based methods are sensitive to measurement scale; large numeric ranges can overwhelm other features.

questions.prompt: Which algorithms are especially sensitive to feature scale? Select all that apply.
options: K-nearest neighbours
K-means
A standard axis-aligned decision tree
A random forest of standard decision trees
questions.explanation: KNN and K-means depend directly on distances. Standard tree splits do not require comparable units across features.

questions.prompt: Which is feature engineering?
options: Deriving family size from sibling and parent counts
Randomly moving test rows into training
Replacing every label with a prediction
Computing the final grade
questions.explanation: Feature engineering constructs useful representations from available inputs.

questions.prompt: Why can adding many irrelevant features harm KNN?
options: Distances can become less informative in a sparse, high-dimensional space
KNN then becomes a neural network
More columns always eliminate noise
The target stops being categorical
questions.explanation: Irrelevant dimensions can dilute meaningful proximity and worsen generalisation.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of comparing unscaled linear-model coefficient magnitudes?
options: Magnitude depends on each feature's measurement units
All coefficients must be positive
Coefficients can never be estimated
Large magnitude proves causation
questions.explanation: A coefficient is a change per unit of its feature, so different units make raw magnitudes misleading as importance scores.

questions.prompt: An hour-of-day feature is derived from a timestamp. Why might it help?
options: It exposes a daily pattern in a form the model can use
It guarantees the absence of time leakage
It proves time causes the target
It removes every seasonal pattern
questions.explanation: Useful transformations can make structure easier to model, but their validity still depends on the prediction setting.

questions.prompt: A churn predictor uses a cancellation reason recorded only after cancellation. What is the issue?
options: Target leakage
A useful prospective predictor
Ordinary class imbalance only
A harmless change of units
questions.explanation: The field contains information unavailable at prediction time and reveals the outcome.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with fitting an imputer on the full dataset before splitting?
options: Held-out information influences the fitted preprocessing
The imputer necessarily becomes a classifier
It doubles every row
Imputation must use test labels only
questions.explanation: Even preprocessing statistics must be learned from training data to preserve the independence of held-out evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which sequence avoids leakage from scaling?
options: Split, fit the scaler on training data, then transform training and test data
Fit on test data, then split
Fit separate scalers on train and test data
Scale using all rows and then hide the target
questions.explanation: Evaluation should apply the transformation learned from training, rather than learning new test-dependent parameters.

questions.prompt: Ten images from each patient appear in a dataset intended for new-patient predictions. Which split is appropriate?
options: Keep all images of each patient in only one split
Randomly scatter each patient's images across all splits
Use patient ID as the target
Duplicate each patient into every split
questions.explanation: A group-aware split prevents patient-specific information from leaking across the evaluation boundary.

questions.prompt: For forecasting future demand, what split best reflects the task?
options: Train on earlier observations and evaluate on later observations
Train on future months and evaluate only on earlier months
Shuffle repeated copies across all splits
Use the target's future value as a feature
questions.explanation: Chronological evaluation simulates predicting the future from information available in the past.

questions.prompt: When should minority-class oversampling be applied?
options: Within the training data, after splitting and inside each CV training fold
To the entire dataset before splitting
Only to the final test set
To every validation label until classes disappear
questions.explanation: Otherwise copies or synthetic examples can contaminate evaluation and give optimistic results.

questions.prompt: What does stratify=y aim to preserve?
options: Similar class proportions across the split
Chronological ordering
A different label for every observation
Equal feature means for all columns
questions.explanation: Stratification approximately preserves class balance; it does not replace group-aware or chronological splitting.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of random_state in a random split?
options: Reproducibility of the split
A guarantee of higher accuracy
Automatic removal of leakage
A guarantee that the sample represents deployment
questions.explanation: A fixed random seed makes comparisons reproducible but does not establish validity.

questions.prompt: Why put preprocessing and the estimator in one pipeline for cross-validation?
options: Each fold learns preprocessing from that fold's training rows
Every fold can safely use the final test labels
It eliminates the need for held-out data
It forces every model to use the same coefficient
questions.explanation: A pipeline helps keep data-dependent transformations within the training boundary of each fold.

questions.prompt: Which features should be investigated for leakage? Select all that apply.
options: A diagnosis recorded after the event being predicted
An aggregate computed using future target outcomes
A measurement genuinely available before prediction
A category known when the user submits the request
questions.explanation: Availability at prediction time matters. Future outcomes must not be smuggled into predictors.

questions.prompt: Two annotators repeatedly disagree about a class. What should the team do first?
options: Clarify the labelling guidelines and inspect ambiguous examples
Assume the model will automatically infer the intended rule
Discard all evaluation data
Increase model depth without inspecting labels
questions.explanation: Inconsistent label definitions introduce noise. Clear guidelines with edge cases improve consistency.

questions.prompt: Does HasCabin=False prove that a passenger had no cabin?
options: No; it may only show that cabin information was not recorded
Yes; missing information is always evidence of absence
Yes; binary features are always ground truth
No; binary features cannot be model inputs
questions.explanation: The notebook's feature encodes recorded information. Interpretation must distinguish missing documentation from confirmed absence.

questions.prompt: Synthetic records help a team test its loading pipeline. What is still unproven?
options: Performance on representative real-world data
Whether the file can be parsed in that test
Whether the program runs on those records
The existence of the synthetic columns
questions.explanation: Synthetic data inherits the generator's assumptions and does not by itself validate deployment performance.

questions.prompt: A model predicts whether a customer leaves next month. Which task is it?
options: Binary classification
Continuous regression
Unlabelled clustering
Dimensionality reduction only
questions.explanation: The output is one of two known categories, leave or stay.

questions.prompt: A transport model predicts bus, tram or metro from labelled journeys. Which task is it?
options: Multiclass classification
Binary classification only
Unsupervised clustering
Continuous regression
questions.explanation: There are more than two predefined target classes.

questions.prompt: Why is logistic regression normally used for classification despite its name?
options: It models class probabilities that can be converted to class labels
It only predicts unrestricted prices
It discovers clusters without labels
It always generates text
questions.explanation: A logistic model maps scores to probabilities and uses a threshold or class comparison for prediction.

questions.prompt: What does a sigmoid function do to a real-valued score?
options: Maps it to a value between zero and one
Always rounds it to an integer greater than one
Sorts observations into clusters
Guarantees that the probability estimate is perfectly calibrated
questions.explanation: The sigmoid bounds outputs for probability modelling but does not guarantee perfect probabilities.

questions.prompt: A binary model returns P(class 1)=0.4 and uses threshold 0.5. What class is predicted?
options: Class 0
Class 1
Both classes with certainty
A third class called 0.4
questions.explanation: The score is below the decision threshold, so the decision rule assigns class 0.

questions.prompt: Which changes can alter a binary classifier's decisions without retraining its weights?
options: Changing the classification threshold
Renaming the saved file only
Printing the same probability twice
Reordering identical input rows without changing their values
questions.explanation: A decision threshold translates fixed probabilities into labels; changing it can change decisions.

questions.prompt: What is a decision boundary?
options: The region separating inputs assigned different classes
The row dividing training files on disk
The maximum allowed size of a CSV file
A guarantee of perfect accuracy
questions.explanation: A boundary describes where the model's predicted class changes in feature space.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes classification from clustering?
options: Classification learns known labels; clustering discovers groups without target labels
Both require the same known class labels
Classification always has two inputs
Clustering always predicts a price
questions.explanation: The distinction is whether target categories are provided during learning.

questions.prompt: What does gradient descent use to update model parameters?
options: The direction that locally reduces the loss
The alphabetical order of labels
Only the final test-set size
The largest feature value regardless of loss
questions.explanation: Gradient descent moves against the loss gradient to seek a lower objective value.

questions.prompt: What is the key simplifying assumption in Naive Bayes?
options: Features are conditionally independent given the class
All classes have equal probability in every dataset
Features are unconditionally identical
The model needs no labelled examples
questions.explanation: The independence assumption is conditional on the target class, not a claim that real-world features never interact.

questions.prompt: In a spam classifier, what is a class prior?
options: The probability of spam before considering the current message's features
The number of words in the current message
The classifier's final threshold only
The probability that every word is independent
questions.explanation: A prior represents baseline class belief before incorporating the observed features.

questions.prompt: In Bayesian classification, what is a posterior?
options: A class probability after incorporating observed evidence
The file size before training
The number of test folds
A categorical feature before encoding
questions.explanation: Bayesian inference combines prior information and likelihoods to update class beliefs.

questions.prompt: Which application is a natural introductory use of Naive Bayes?
options: Classifying text from word-related features
Computing a deterministic CSV separator
Discovering K-means centroids
Drawing a regression line without a target
questions.explanation: Naive Bayes is commonly used as a simple text classifier with feature likelihoods conditioned on class.

questions.prompt: Two strongly related word features occur together. What limitation matters for Naive Bayes?
options: Its independence approximation may count related evidence as if independent
It necessarily stops producing predictions
It becomes an unsupervised model
Its outputs always become perfectly accurate
questions.explanation: Dependence can violate the simplifying assumption, although the classifier may still be useful.

questions.prompt: What does a support vector classifier seek in its basic linear form?
options: A separating hyperplane with a large margin
The mean of every unlabelled cluster only
A single memorised text response
A line that predicts all continuous targets exactly
questions.explanation: The SVM margin expresses separation between classes; support vectors are influential near-boundary examples.

questions.prompt: Why is feature scaling relevant to an SVM?
options: Feature units affect its geometry and margin
Scaling creates missing target labels
Every SVM is an axis-aligned tree
Scaling guarantees the classes are separable
questions.explanation: Comparably scaled features help prevent a large-scale measurement from dominating distance-related geometry.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the SVM family is correct?
options: It includes methods for classification and regression
It can only predict text tokens
It is inherently a clustering-only family
It never uses input features
questions.explanation: Support vector classification and support vector regression address different supervised outputs.

questions.prompt: A dataset has two input dimensions. What is a linear decision boundary in that space?
options: A line
A three-dimensional volume
A single class probability for the whole dataset
The entire training table
questions.explanation: In two dimensions, a hyperplane separating classes is a one-dimensional line.

questions.prompt: Which are reasonable considerations when selecting an SVM? Select all that apply.
options: Feature scale
Training cost as the dataset grows
A guarantee of instant training on any dataset
A guarantee of native calibrated probabilities in every configuration
questions.explanation: The slides discuss scaling, computational cost and probability estimation as practical considerations.

questions.prompt: For ordinary unweighted KNN classification, how is a new sample labelled?
options: By a majority vote among its K closest labelled examples
By the average of all target category names
By fitting a deep network at every call
By assigning the largest numeric feature as its class
questions.explanation: KNN uses neighbouring training labels and a distance measure to classify a query.

questions.prompt: What is stored during the basic KNN fitting stage?
options: The training examples and labels used for neighbour search
Only a single global linear slope
Only the final confusion matrix
A separate label for every future query
questions.explanation: KNN defers much of the work to prediction, when it searches the stored examples.

questions.prompt: What is a common risk of K=1?
options: Sensitivity to noise and isolated training examples
An inability to create flexible boundaries
A guarantee of low variance
Automatic removal of every outlier
questions.explanation: A single neighbour can reflect noise, leading to a highly local and unstable decision rule.

questions.prompt: What can happen if K is made extremely large?
options: Local class patterns can be smoothed away
Every training outlier gets its own exact rule
The model becomes more sensitive to one nearest point
The feature scales cease to matter
questions.explanation: Large neighbourhoods can reduce variance but introduce bias by ignoring local structure.

questions.prompt: Where should K be selected?
options: On validation data or through cross-validation
By repeatedly maximising the final test score
From the test labels after deployment
By choosing the highest training score alone
questions.explanation: K is a hyperparameter. Model-selection data should be separate from final evaluation data.

questions.prompt: Why can KNN prediction become expensive with a large training set?
options: Many stored examples may need to be searched for neighbours
It must label the test set by hand
It always trains a new random forest
It only works with a single row
questions.explanation: Neighbour search can require substantial computation as stored data grows.

questions.prompt: Which changes could plausibly help a poor KNN model? Select all that apply.
options: Scale features using training statistics
Tune K on validation data
Include the hidden test target as a feature
Duplicate test samples into the training set
questions.explanation: Scaling and hyperparameter selection are valid interventions; leakage would invalidate the score.

questions.prompt: What is a leaf in a classification tree?
options: A terminal region that supplies a prediction
The name of the full dataset
A newly collected training label
The validation algorithm itself
questions.explanation: A prediction follows feature tests from the root until a terminal node is reached.

questions.prompt: Which split is preferred by an impurity-based tree, all else equal?
options: One that produces purer child groups
One that intentionally mixes labels as much as possible
One chosen only by feature name
One that uses future test outcomes
questions.explanation: Impurity criteria such as Gini or entropy reward better class separation in the children.

questions.prompt: A tree memorises training rows but performs poorly on unseen data. Which change can help?
options: Limit its depth or increase minimum leaf size
Add the test labels as a feature
Force every training point into a separate leaf
Choose the model with the highest training accuracy only
questions.explanation: Constraining complexity can reduce overfitting and improve generalisation.

questions.prompt: What is the central idea of a random forest classifier?
options: Combine votes from multiple varied decision trees
Use one neighbour with no labels
Fit one line to a continuous output only
Remove all randomness from tree construction
questions.explanation: An ensemble of trees can be more stable than an individual tree.

questions.prompt: Why is a shallow decision tree often easier to inspect than a large ensemble?
options: Its prediction path can be expressed as a short sequence of rules
It has no parameters or decisions
It always has better accuracy
It proves causal relationships
questions.explanation: A short path of feature tests is relatively interpretable, although interpretability does not establish accuracy or causality.

questions.prompt: Which are tree-complexity controls? Select all that apply.
options: Maximum depth
Minimum number of samples per leaf
Renaming the predicted label
Changing the chart colour
questions.explanation: These controls constrain splitting and the size of terminal regions.

questions.prompt: What does model.fit(X_train, y_train) normally do in supervised learning?
options: Learns model parameters from training inputs and targets
Measures final test accuracy without training
Predicts labels without accessing the target
Creates a new exam attempt
questions.explanation: fit estimates a mapping from the supplied training examples.

questions.prompt: After fitting, what does model.predict(X_test) return for a classifier?
options: Predicted labels for the test inputs
The correct hidden labels by definition
A new set of training features
A guarantee that every prediction is correct
questions.explanation: Prediction applies the learned model; comparison to y_test is a separate evaluation step.

questions.prompt: A classifier has 100% training accuracy. What additional evidence is needed to assess generalisation?
options: Performance on representative held-out data
The filename alone
The order of class names
Proof that training took many hours
questions.explanation: Training performance may reflect memorisation and does not establish unseen-data performance.

questions.prompt: Which steps belong to the supervised ML workflow? Select all that apply.
options: Define the target and available features
Evaluate on unseen examples
Select the best model using the final test labels repeatedly
Assume monitoring is unnecessary after deployment
questions.explanation: Good workflow starts with task definition and includes independent evaluation and later monitoring.

questions.prompt: Predicting a house's sale price in kroner is primarily which task?
options: Regression
Binary classification
Unsupervised clustering
Association-rule mining
questions.explanation: The target is a numeric quantity, so regression is an appropriate formulation.

questions.prompt: The same stock dataset can support two tasks. Which target makes it classification?
options: Whether tomorrow's closing price rises or falls
Tomorrow's exact closing price
The size of tomorrow's price change in kroner
Tomorrow's trading volume as a number
questions.explanation: The rise/fall target is categorical; the other formulations request numeric values.

questions.prompt: In y = a + bx, what is the intercept a?
options: The model's predicted y when x is zero
The amount y changes for each unit increase of x
The number of observations
The final test error
questions.explanation: The intercept is a model quantity; whether x=0 is meaningful depends on the data domain.

questions.prompt: In a multiple linear model, how is one coefficient interpreted?
options: Predicted output change per unit of that feature, holding other inputs fixed
The model's entire error rate
The probability that the feature causes the outcome
The number of training samples with that value
questions.explanation: The interpretation is conditional on the other model inputs and is not automatically causal.

questions.prompt: A regression coefficient is negative. What does the model predict when that input increases, with others fixed?
options: The predicted output decreases
The predicted output must become negative
The loss is necessarily negative
The feature is necessarily useless
questions.explanation: A negative coefficient specifies a decreasing conditional linear relationship, not the sign of the overall prediction.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes simple from multiple linear regression?
options: One input feature versus several input features
Two classes versus many classes
No targets versus known targets
No fitting versus fitting
questions.explanation: Both predict numeric targets; the difference is the number of predictors.

questions.prompt: A model trained on journeys of 1–5 km predicts a 200 km trip. What deserves caution?
options: Extrapolation beyond the observed input range
A guarantee that longer trips obey the fitted local pattern
The absence of any numeric target
The impossibility of making any numeric prediction
questions.explanation: The learned relationship may not hold far outside the observed range.

questions.prompt: Can a linear regression fit produce negative predictions?
options: Yes; ordinary linear regression does not constrain its output range
No; all regressors use sigmoid
No; regression predicts only known classes
Only if every coefficient is negative
questions.explanation: An unconstrained linear combination can take negative values even when such values are implausible for the task.

questions.prompt: Why add x² as a regression feature?
options: To allow a curved relationship with x
To turn all targets into binary labels
To guarantee perfect generalisation
To remove the need for fitting
questions.explanation: Polynomial features let a linear-in-coefficients model express nonlinear shapes in the original input.

questions.prompt: A very high-degree polynomial fits every training point but oscillates between them. What is a likely concern?
options: Overfitting
Guaranteed low variance
A missing classification threshold only
Too few fitted parameters by definition
questions.explanation: Excessive flexibility can fit noise and generalise poorly.

questions.prompt: With residual defined as actual minus predicted, what does a positive residual indicate?
options: The prediction was too low
The prediction was too high
The prediction was exact
The predicted class was positive
questions.explanation: A positive actual-minus-predicted difference means the observation exceeded the prediction.

questions.prompt: Why is the mean signed residual a poor measure of typical error size?
options: Positive and negative errors can cancel
Residuals cannot be calculated
It always equals accuracy
It gives extra weight to every large error
questions.explanation: Cancellation can hide large individual errors. Absolute or squared errors avoid this issue.

questions.prompt: What units does MAE have?
options: The same units as the target
Squared target units
No units for any target
The units of the row index
questions.explanation: MAE averages absolute differences between predictions and observations.

questions.prompt: Compared with MAE, why does MSE emphasise large errors?
options: It squares each error before averaging
It ignores all small predictions
It counts only the number of rows
It replaces the target with its rank
questions.explanation: Squaring increases the relative contribution of larger residuals.

questions.prompt: What does RMSE do to MSE?
options: Takes its square root, restoring target units
Divides it by the number of features
Turns it into classification accuracy
Replaces all large errors with zero
questions.explanation: RMSE remains sensitive to large errors while being expressed in the target's units.

questions.prompt: Can held-out R² be negative?
options: Yes; predictions can be worse in squared error than the held-out mean baseline
No; every regression score is a probability
No; R² is always the same as accuracy
Only when all targets are negative
questions.explanation: R² = 1 − residual sum of squares / total sum of squares, which can be below zero.

questions.prompt: For nonconstant evaluation targets, what does R²=0 mean?
options: The residual squared-error sum equals that of predicting their mean
Every prediction is correct
Every prediction equals zero
The model has no coefficients
questions.explanation: R² compares squared errors against the evaluation-target mean reference.

questions.prompt: Which are regression evaluation measures? Select all that apply.
options: MAE
RMSE
Binary recall
Binary precision
questions.explanation: MAE and RMSE assess numeric prediction errors; precision and recall assess positive-class decisions.

questions.prompt: Two regressors have the same MAE but different RMSE. What can explain this?
options: One has a few larger errors and many smaller ones
They must have identical residuals
RMSE is unrelated to residuals
MAE counts only correct class labels
questions.explanation: Different error distributions can have the same mean absolute size but different mean squares.

questions.prompt: Why compare regression performance against a simple baseline?
options: To judge whether modelling improves on an inexpensive reference
To guarantee a high R²
To remove the need for representative test data
To make the training labels unnecessary
questions.explanation: A baseline provides context for whether the learned relationship adds useful predictive value.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of a fitted price coefficient is justified?
options: It describes the model's association conditional on other inputs
It proves a physical intervention will cause exactly that price change
It is independent of feature units
It is the test-set size
questions.explanation: Predictive regression coefficients do not, by themselves, identify causal effects.

questions.prompt: Which checks help assess a regression model? Select all that apply.
options: Compare predicted and actual values on held-out data
Inspect residual patterns
Report training fit as the only evidence
Treat any nonzero R² as proof of causation
questions.explanation: Held-out errors and residual structure reveal predictive weaknesses; training fit alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: What information is absent in a standard clustering task?
options: Preassigned target group labels for training
All input features
Every distance measure
All observations
questions.explanation: Clustering uses feature structure to discover groups rather than learning provided class labels.

questions.prompt: An algorithm groups commuters using trip length and departure time. What should happen before naming the groups?
options: Inspect their characteristics and practical meaning
Assume the cluster IDs are official social categories
Treat every group as a causal explanation
Assign group names from the numeric ID alone
questions.explanation: Clusters require interpretation and may reflect measurement choices or collection artefacts.

questions.prompt: Why can changing the chosen clustering features change the groups?
options: Similarity is defined using those features
Cluster membership is independent of data representation
Every feature set defines the same distances
The target labels force identical groups
questions.explanation: Clustering structure depends on what is measured and how similarity is computed.

questions.prompt: Which are valid cautions about clustering? Select all that apply.
options: Groups may reflect collection artefacts
Scaling can affect distance-based groups
Every cluster is necessarily a real social category
The algorithm proves the groups are causally distinct
questions.explanation: Discovered patterns need domain validation and can depend strongly on data representation.

questions.prompt: In K-means, what does K specify?
options: The requested number of clusters
The number of nearest labels voting on a query
The number of target classes supplied as labels
The number of test examples
questions.explanation: K-means seeks K groups; KNN uses a similarly named parameter for a different purpose.

questions.prompt: What happens in the assignment step of K-means?
options: Each observation is assigned to its nearest current centroid
Every label is replaced by a test prediction
The farthest pair is deleted
All observations become separate clusters
questions.explanation: The algorithm alternates nearest-centre assignment and centre updates.

questions.prompt: How is a K-means centroid updated?
options: Take the arithmetic mean of its assigned observations
Choose the largest target label
Use the first test observation automatically
Set all coordinates to zero
questions.explanation: For squared Euclidean distance, the mean minimises within-cluster squared distances for a fixed assignment.

questions.prompt: Must a K-means centroid coincide with an observed point?
options: No; a mean can lie between observations
Yes; it must be the first observation
Yes; a centroid is always a class label
No; centroids cannot have coordinates
questions.explanation: A centroid is a representative location and may not correspond to any actual data row.

questions.prompt: What is a usual K-means stopping condition?
options: Centres or assignments stabilise, or an iteration limit is reached
Every cluster has a human-provided target label
Accuracy reaches exactly 100%
All features become text
questions.explanation: K-means iterates until further changes are small or the configured computation limit is met.

questions.prompt: Why try several initialisations in K-means?
options: Different starting centres can lead to different local solutions
Every initialisation changes the target definition
It guarantees a unique global optimum in every dataset
Initialisation has no effect on optimisation
questions.explanation: The optimisation can settle in different local minima depending on its starting positions.

questions.prompt: What can happen if income is left unscaled alongside a small-range feature in K-means?
options: Income differences can dominate cluster assignment
Income is automatically ignored
K-means becomes independent of distance
The model becomes supervised
questions.explanation: The same scaling issue that affects KNN affects K-means distances.

questions.prompt: Why can a large outlier move a K-means centroid substantially?
options: A mean is sensitive to extreme values
A centroid is always a median
Outliers are automatically labelled as noise by K-means
The number of classes determines the outlier's value
questions.explanation: K-means updates centres using means and can be distorted by extreme observations.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits K-means' typical geometric preference?
options: Compact groups around centres under its distance measure
Arbitrary-shaped chains with guaranteed noise rejection
Groups defined exclusively by target labels
A hierarchy of every possible partition
questions.explanation: K-means is naturally suited to compact, roughly spherical groups in appropriately scaled Euclidean feature space.

questions.prompt: Which steps are part of K-means? Select all that apply.
options: Assign points to nearest centres
Recompute centres from assigned points
Request true class labels at every iteration
Evaluate a logistic sigmoid for each centroid
questions.explanation: The defining cycle alternates assignment and mean updates without requiring target labels.

questions.prompt: What is the central idea of mean shift?
options: Move a local window towards a dense region of observations
Fit one supervised slope to all targets
Vote using exactly K target labels
Split a decision tree by Gini impurity
questions.explanation: Mean shift repeatedly moves towards local concentrations of data.

questions.prompt: Which mean-shift setting controls the scale of its neighbourhood?
options: Bandwidth
The regression intercept
The final grade threshold
The class label name
questions.explanation: Bandwidth determines the spatial window and affects which density peaks are discovered.

questions.prompt: Does mean shift normally require the number of clusters in advance?
options: No; bandwidth influences how many density peaks emerge
Yes; it is defined only for exactly two clusters
Yes; it requires every point's true class
No; it produces no groups
questions.explanation: The number of groups emerges from the density structure at the selected bandwidth.

questions.prompt: How does DBSCAN handle sufficiently isolated observations?
options: It can mark them as noise
It must force them into one of K predefined clusters
It assigns the largest class label
It always deletes the corresponding feature
questions.explanation: DBSCAN separates dense groups and can leave observations outside them as noise.

questions.prompt: Which settings directly control DBSCAN's density criterion?
options: Neighbourhood radius and minimum neighbourhood size
Learning rate and regression slope
Tree depth and leaf count
Precision and recall thresholds only
questions.explanation: The radius determines nearby points; the minimum count determines whether a sufficiently dense region exists.

questions.prompt: Why might DBSCAN be useful for irregularly shaped groups?
options: It connects dense neighbourhoods rather than relying only on distance to a centroid
It always assumes spherical groups
